newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-MOUNTAIN MAN MYLLYLAE REACHES HIS PEAK.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-MOUNTAIN MAN MYLLYLAE REACHES HIS PEAK.

text.p: Finn Mika Myllylae, a keen mountaineer who once climbed Mount McKinley, reached another personal peak by winning Sunday's 50-km race at the Nordic skiing world championships.
"This was my expedition of the year," said Myllylae, who uses his spare times to climb summits in Alaska or elsewhere with friend and team mate Jari Isometsae.
"My next mountain will be Nagano," added the 27-year-old Finn, already thinking about next year's Olympics.
Until Sunday, Myllylae had been in the shadow of Bjorn Daehlie, collecting two silvers and one bronze in the 10-day festival while the great Norwegian picked up three golds.
But in the grand finale, Myllylae was in front at last, moving almost effortlessly despite pouring rain and sticky snow.
"It's a miracle," he said after winning 54.90 seconds ahead of Norwegian Erling Jevne with a tiring Daehlie third 1:58.50 back.

"The conditions were really tough today and when I woke up this morning and saw what the weather was like, I thought I wouldn't make it," he added. "I had a new pair of skis which I had never used before and I was afraid about the waxing but in the end, everything was just fine."
Myllylae, a powerful athlete with great determination, had not won much until a few months ago. But this winter, he proved he was up there with the best by posting two wins on the World Cup circuit.

"That put me under a lot of pressure," said Myllylae, the first Finn to win the 50-km race in a major competition since Kalevi Oikarainen in the 1970 world championships in Visoke Tatry, now in the Czech Republic. "All the people at home expected me to win a gold and I wasn't sure I would make it."
More at ease in the solitude of Finnish forests than before live audiences, Myllylae goes by the nickname of Karpaasit.
"It's hard to translate," he said. "A karpaasit is a man who lives in the forests and hunts for food. He loves nature and he's a quiet man. I guess I'm a bit like that."

Myllylae was raised in the south of Sweden, where snow is scarce. He started skiing at the age of four, but his main sport was athletics. Then, when he was 11, he moved to Finland with his family and cross-country skiing became his passion.
"When I was a kid, I dreamt that maybe, one day, I would win a world title or an Olympic gold medal," he said. "This is really a dream come true."
Over the last few years, Finland have been regularly outclassed by neighbours Norway in Nordic skiing. Myllylae said he hoped his win would change that.
"We are a strong team with several talented skiers," he said. "Maybe my win will boost our confidence and make us believe that we can beat the Norwegians."
Daehlie, sitting by his side in the conference room, smiled. A few days earlier, he had heard a helpless Myllylae call him "a man from another planet."
"Mika eventually found out that I was not unbeatable," Daehlie said. "Today, he was the man from Mars."
